questions.question: How do you write a custom hook in React? Give a useFetch example.
questions.title: Custom Hooks in React — How to Write Them (useFetch Example)
questions.direct_answer:
How do you write a custom hook in React? Give a useFetch example.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Functions starting with use, composing built-in hooks, returning state + actions; exhaustive-deps respect; AbortController for fetch.

**Classic weak answer:** Forgetting to clean up async operations on unmount — the returned fetch may set state on an unmounted component.

**Senior finish:** Build a useFetch with loading/data/error, AbortController on unmount, and dependency-aware refetch.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **Custom Hooks in React — How to Write Them (useFetch Example)** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** How do you write a custom hook in React? Give a useFetch example.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Functions starting with use, composing built-in hooks, returning state + actions; exhaustive-deps respect; AbortController for fetch**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Forgetting to clean up async operations on unmount — the returned fetch may set state on an unmounted component**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Build a useFetch with loading/data/error, AbortController on unmount, and dependency-aware refetch**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Functions starting with use, composing built-in hooks, returning state + actions; exhaustive-deps respect; AbortController for fetch
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **forgetting to clean up async operations on unmount — the returned fetch may set state on an unmounted component** and what you do instead.

questions.question: What are the rules of React hooks? Why do they exist?
questions.title: Rules of React Hooks — Why They Exist (Top-Level, Same Order)
questions.direct_answer:
What are the rules of React hooks? Why do they exist?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Only call hooks at the top level and from React functions; the rules enforce consistent call order so React can track state positionally.

**Classic weak answer:** Calling a hook inside an if/for/early-return — breaks state order and triggers the 'rendered more/fewer hooks' error.

**Senior finish:** Reference the eslint-plugin-react-hooks rule of hooks and how React Compiler relaxes some manual concerns (memoization) but not the call-order rule.

interviewer_intent.testing: Only call hooks at the top level and from React functions; the rules enforce consistent call order so React can track state positionally

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference the eslint-plugin-react-hooks rule of hooks and how React Compiler relaxes some manual concerns (memoization) but not the call-order rule
